div.p:
The oppressive military burden under which Europe is at present groaning has been imposed upon it principally by the French Republic. The hope and desire to exhaust Germany financially have been frequently expressed in France by forcing it to constant and heavy military expenses. “The financial war,” as it was called, was principally waged against the hated neighbor. The recent disturbances in France plainly show that the sword with which French diplomatists have been playing for years, was a two-edged one. France has burdened herself with a constantly increasing budget which her increasing income even cannot balance. The lion’s share of these expenses
falls to fortifications, the army and navy, and foreign enterprises. Little remains for the advancement of the public welfare.

The Republic, in her present martial array, fears the danger of succumbing to Cӕsarism within her. The discontent arising from the neglect of the interests of the working classes, the pressure which the heavy, indirect taxes impose upon them, is finding expression in the socialistic anarchist movement, and already voices are heard clamoring for the protection of the sword. French statesmen have fostered these socialistic dangers by their unfortunate military diplomacy.

The other European states, and principally Germany, are made to suffer for the military armaments of France. It is very natural for the working classes to see the cause of all their privations in the course pursued by Gambetta. If France, made wiser by the present events, should precede Europe in a partial disarmament, a step which the rest of Europe would certainly follow, she would not only thereby really place herself at the head of civilization, but would protect her present institutions from the danger of imperialism. It would also confer an incomparable blessing upon the poorer and suffering portion of Europe. How much good could be done by France and the other states with the millions which are now swallowed up by the military budget, if a treaty looking to a partial disarmament were agreed upon. If France persists in closing her ears to the warning given her in the recent disturbances, and continues by her insensate armament to exhaust her own power and that of Europe, the danger will certainly, sooner or later, recoil upon her head.
